title: Jasmine After Rain
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 40 of 40
content:
After the rain, the Jasmine Dragon smelled of wet brick and orange peel.

I found Iroh standing beside the window, watching water slide down the outside of the glass. The street below was crowded with people stepping around puddles. A cart wheel struck a loose paving stone and sent a little spray over its driver's boots.

Iroh winced in sympathy.

"That stone needs to be reset," I said.

"Yes. And if I go outside to reset it now, Mina will remind me the shop's roof needs attention first."

"She's right."

"An alarming trend."

I smiled.

We had spent the past week repairing small things: a leaking gutter, an uneven shelf, a stubborn back door that swelled whenever it rained. The projects weren't glorious. There were receipts, delays and arguments about whether the money could stretch to one more patch before the season changed.

Iroh had treated each task with the same serious care he once might have given a diplomatic mission. He was learning to say when he was tired; I was learning not to hear every unfinished job as an accusation.

The shop had only just reopened after the rain.

Mina came from the kitchen with a handwritten list.

"The supplier delivered enough ginger for two days, not three," she said. "If we serve the special all weekend, we'll run out before the next cart."

Iroh studied the sheet.

"Then we shall limit the special."

"Please tell the customers," Mina said.

"Of course."

She looked between us.

"And please don't spend the afternoon arguing about whose turn it is to climb onto the roof."

Iroh's mouth twitched.

"Your faith in my judgment is touching."

"I trust your judgment. I don't trust that ladder."

She returned to the kitchen.

I went to the notice board and wrote the updated menu. The change was boring, practical and necessary. We had enough ingredients for the house blend, and the regular customers could still come in from the wet street to drink something warm.

The first person through the door was Halen.

He stopped beneath the awning, shaking rain from his sleeves.

"Did I miss the special?"

"Not yet," I said. "There are a few servings left today."

He nodded, then pointed at the window table.

"Is that one free?"

I looked to Iroh. Halen had been coming less often since his sister died. We didn't have the right to turn every visit into a conversation about grief.

"It's free," Iroh said. "Would you like it?"

"Yes, please."

He sat. We served his tea, then left him to look out at the rain.

Iroh watched the street for another moment.

"Do you ever feel that the shop asks too much of us?" he asked quietly.

"Sometimes. Not always."

He looked at the door.

"I spent so many years moving away from places where people needed me to be a general. I thought a small shop would make it simple to stay."

"Has it?"

"No." He smiled faintly. "I have discovered that people can need a great many things from a man who only meant to sell tea."

"You're allowed to decide what you can offer."

"I know you keep telling me."

"I'm going to keep telling you until you believe it."

He took my hand, then seemed to think better of it because Mina was calling for help with the dry-goods shelf. He looked torn between the room and the kitchen.

"Go help her," I said. "I'll watch the counter."

"Would you mind?"

"No. But come back after. We need to talk about next week."

His expression changed.

"Is something wrong?"

"Not wrong. A plan."

He nodded and went to the back.

I served two customers and counted the remaining portions of ginger before lowering the special's availability on the menu. The afternoon passed in the comforting rhythm of a business that could run without becoming a shrine to anyone's past.

When Iroh returned, he carried a short piece of wood.

"What's that?" I asked.

"The shelf support. It was less heroic than it appeared."

"Did you fix it?"

"Mina did. I held the shelf."

I laughed.

We closed early when the street flooded again near the market corner. Nobody was trapped; the posted upper route remained open. The safer decision was to clean, bring the outdoor sign inside and let the rain pass.

Iroh made two cups of tea. We sat at the table where we had first argued about whether happiness was another thing a person had to deserve.

"I'll be crossing to Lanternweald next week," I said. "There is a scheduled meeting about the shared drainage. Afterward I have time with Maui, and a visit to Moonroot."

He looked at his cup.

"Thank you for telling me."

"I wanted to ask about our next date before I put anything on the calendar."

He considered.

"Thursday evening. I can close at six if Mina wishes to take the late shift."

"Only if she agrees. And only if she gets the hours she actually wants."

"Of course."

I studied him.

"Are you worried?"

He laughed without much humor.

"I seem to have spent most of my life expecting a good thing to be taken away."

"Do you think me loving other people means I'm going to stop loving you?"

"No." He met my eyes. "But there are days when knowing something and feeling it are not the same."

I took a slow breath.

"I'm ethically non-monogamous. I prefer polyamory. I told you that before we began, and I meant it. I also mean it when I say I want to come back here. I don't want to promise I'm never going to miss a train or have a difficult conversation. I want us to be able to say when it hurts."

He nodded.

"And I must not turn the hurt into a command."

"Neither of us should."

He looked out at the wet street.

"Perhaps this is what frightened me most. Happiness used to feel like a debt. If I enjoyed it, I believed something would be expected of me in return."

"What would you like it to be now?"

He took my hand across the table.

"A cup of tea. A date we agree to. The freedom to tell you when I am afraid."

I smiled.

"That sounds manageable."

"Not always."

"No. But real."

He leaned toward me.

"May I kiss you?"

"Yes."

The kiss was gentle at first. When I reached up to touch his cheek, he smiled against my mouth. The kettle began to whistle, as if it objected to being ignored.

I laughed.

Iroh sighed.

"Even my kitchen insists upon participating."

We turned off the stove, put away the cups and closed the shutters. Upstairs, the room smelled faintly of cedar. We left the rest of the evening unwritten, ours to keep.

Before going upstairs, we heard a knock at the service door. It was Bo from Jasmine Steps, carrying a clipboard speckled with rain and a folded notice from the district works office.

“The lane behind your shop is going to close tomorrow,” Bo said. “They found a cracked drain collar by the tea deliveries.”

Iroh took the notice. “The closure is sensible.”

“Good. Because two vendors have already asked me to ignore it for the morning rush.”

He almost smiled. “A familiar temptation.”

Bo spread the map across the counter. The alternate delivery route passed a narrow ramp used by the clinic and the upstairs residents. Heavy carts would make it impassable.

“Could we move the cart times?” I asked.

“Only if the drivers agree and somebody pays them for the early start,” Bo replied. “The works office isn't doing that.”

Iroh reached for the ledger. I saw the old instinct assemble a plan in his expression, but this time he started with a question.

“Who should be at the discussion?”

“Drivers. Clinic. Mina. The vendors who'll lose the morning slot. Then us.”

We wrote their names on separate slips instead of putting them into a timetable. Bo agreed to deliver invitations, not assignments. Mina, who had been listening from the kitchen, insisted that any new delivery hour appear on the paid rota. Iroh opened the cash drawer, checked the sum, and said that the special could wait until the road was safe.

When Bo left, I stood near the kettle with a slip of paper between my fingers. It said *ask before deciding*. The ink had spread slightly where I'd touched it.

“Somewhat less romantic than a lantern festival,” I said.

Iroh came close enough for me to feel the warmth of his shoulder. “A safe kitchen has its charms.”

“That's a dreadful line.”

“It was never intended for publication.”

I kissed him before he could improve it. He tasted of the last cup of tea, and for once the interruption at the door had left us with work we could share rather than a crisis he had to solve alone.


In the morning the clouds had opened. Light shone on the wet street and the old paving stone.

Mina arrived with a carpenter's estimate for the roof.

"Before you offer to climb anything," she said, "read this."

Iroh did.

Then he reached for the shop ledger and began to work out how to pay for it.

The rain had ended. The work hadn't. Neither had our life together.

bridge_outro: The Jasmine Steps gained a tea stall the following spring. It was not a replacement for the Jasmine Dragon; the real shop waited beyond its door, complete with customers who knew exactly how their cups should be filled. Here, though, Iroh could sit with people who knew him without any need for legends. Greg arrived with his guitar, Katara with a basket of herbs, and Severus with a severe opinion about steeping times. Iroh set out more cups than he needed. He did not ask anyone to stay forever. When I reached for his hand beneath the counter, the square felt less like an escape than a place where the roads of several lives met.
